title: Cheapest Drop Through a Grid
statement:
You get an n × n grid of integers. A drop starts at any cell of the top row and moves down one row at a time until it reaches the bottom row. From column c it may move to column c − 1, c or c + 1 of the next row, as long as that column exists.

The cost of a drop is the sum of every cell it visits, top and bottom included. Return the smallest possible cost. Values can be negative.

examples.why: 1 → 2 → 4. Starting from the smallest top cell is right here, but only because a cheap path continues from it.
2 → -5 → 9. Greedily taking the 1 at the top leads to a 9 in the second row; the path through -5 is cheaper overall.
One cell is both the top and the bottom row.

gen: (r, big) => { const n = big ? 100 : r.int(1, 5); return [r.matrix(n, n, -100, 100)]; }
hints: Choosing the cheapest next cell at each step does not work. What do you need to know about a cell to decide correctly?
Let best[r][c] be the cheapest cost of a drop that ends at cell (r, c). It depends only on three cells of row r − 1.
best[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(best[r−1][c−1], best[r−1][c], best[r−1][c+1]), skipping columns that do not exist. The answer is the minimum of the last row. One row of memory is enough.

explain.intuition:
A greedy drop looks only one step ahead, so a cheap cell can lead it into an expensive row. Turn the question around: for each cell, what is the cheapest way to arrive there? A cell can only be reached from the three cells above it, so its cheapest arrival is its own value plus the cheapest of those three.

Fill row by row from the top. Each row needs only the previous row, so you keep one array and replace it as you go. The answer is the smallest value in the final row.
steps: Copy the top row into prev: arriving at the top costs just the cell itself.
For each next row r and column c, take the smallest of prev[c − 1], prev[c], prev[c + 1] that exist.
Set cur[c] = grid[r][c] + that minimum. After the row, prev = cur.
pitfalls: Picking the smallest top cell and then the cheapest neighbour each step. Example 2 shows it loses.
Updating prev in place while scanning a row. prev[c − 1] is then already overwritten when column c needs it.
Returning prev[0] or the last cell instead of the minimum over the whole bottom row.

solutions.title: Try every path
solutions.idea: Recurse from every top cell into all three children and keep the cheapest total.

solutions.title: Row-by-row DP
solutions.idea: The cheapest arrival at a cell is its value plus the cheapest of the up to three cells above it. Keep only the previous row.

followups: Forbid the drop from staying in the same column on two consecutive rows. How does each cell's update change, and can it stay O(n²)?
Also return the columns of one cheapest path.
